NATURE OF THE DECISION 2
Petitioners appeal a city council decision on remand from Haystack Rock, 3 LLC v. Cannon Beach, ___ Or LUBA ___ (LUBA No 2022-041, Mar 16, 2023) 4 (Haystack Rock) denying a development permit for a single-family dwelling and 5 associated vehicular access and tree removal. 6
BACKGROUND 7
The subject property is a 5,394-square-foot lot on a steep hillside facing 8 the Pacific Ocean in the Tolovana Park Subdivision. The property is vacant and 9 is zoned Residential Lower Density (RL) with an Oceanfront Management (OM) 10 overlay. The property slopes towards the ocean. To the east of the subject 11 property is South Hemlock Street. Petitioners propose vehicular access to the 12 proposed dwelling from South Hemlock Street via Nenana Avenue, an 13 undeveloped right-of-way dedicated to the city in the 1908 Tolovana Park 14 Subdivision plat.1 15

Petitioners proposed to provide vehicular 7 access by constructing a paved surface over the Nenana Avenue right-of-way 8 from South Hemlock Street to the parking area. MOTIONS TO TAKE OFFICIAL NOTICE AND MOTIONS TO STRIKE 4

A. Oceanfront Management Overlay Zone Regulations 4
We set out the legal framework that the city applied as useful context 5 before describing petitioners’ specific challenges. 6
“The intent of the oceanfront management overlay (OM) zone is to 7 regulate uses and activities in the affected areas in order to: ensure 8 that development is consistent with the natural limitations of the 9 oceanshore; to ensure that identified recreational, aesthetic, wildlife 10 habitat and other resources are protected; to conserve, protect, where 11 appropriate develop, and where appropriate restore the resources 12 and benefits of beach and dune areas; and to reduce the hazards to 13 property and human life resulting from both natural events and 14 development activities.” CBMC 17.42.010. 15
Uses and activities within the OM zone are subject to the provisions and 16 standards of the underlying zone and CBMC 17.42. Where the provisions of the 17 OM overlay zone and the underlying zone conflict, the provisions of the OM 18 overlay zone prevail. CBMC 17.42.020(B). 19
CBMC 17.42.030 identifies “uses and activities” that are permitted “for 20 lots or right-of-way” in the OM zone and provides, in part: 21
“D. For lots or right-of-way that do not consist of a beach, active 22 dunes, or other foredunes which are conditionally stable and that are 23 subject to wave overtopping or ocean undercutting, or interdune 24 areas that are subject to ocean flooding: in addition to the uses 25 permitted in the underlying zone, the following uses and activities 26 are permitted subject to provisions of Section 17.92.010, 27 Development permits: 28 Page 16
“1. Private beach access improvements, subject to the provisions 1 of Section 17.42.060(A)(7); 2
“2. Maintenance and repair to existing shoreline stabilization 3 structure, subject to the provisions of Section 17.80.230(K); 4
“3. Remedial dune grading. 5
“E. For lots or right-of-way that do not consist of a beach, active 6 dunes, or other foredunes which are conditionally stable and that are 7 subject to wave overtopping or ocean undercutting, or interdune 8 areas that are subject to ocean flooding: in addition to the uses 9 permitted in the underlying zone, the following uses and activities 10 are permitted subject to provision of Chapter 17.44, Design Review: 11
“1. Public beach access improvements, subject to the provisions 12 of Section 17.42.060(A)(7); 13
“2. Stormwater outfalls or facilities, which may include 14 infiltration or water quality systems.” (Boldface omitted; 15 emphases added.) 16
CBMC 17.42.040 identifies “uses and activities” that are prohibited in the 17 OM zone. Residential development is “prohibited on beaches, active dunes, or 18 other foredunes which are conditionally stable and that are subject to wave 19 overtopping or ocean undercutting, or interdune areas that are subject to ocean 20 flooding.” CBMC 17.42.040(A). It is undisputed that petitioners do not propose 21 any development prohibited by CBMC 17.42.040(A). 22
“The uses and activities permitted in all areas contained in the OM zone 23 are subject to the [standards in CBMC 17.42.050].” CBMC 17.42.050(A). All 24 uses and activities are subject to the geologic hazard area requirements in CBMC 25 17.50. CBMC 17.42.050(A)(2). 26 Page 17
“[A]ll lots abutting the oceanshore” are subject to an oceanfront setback 1 standard establishing the “ocean yard,” in which most development is prohibited. 2 CBMC 17.42.050(A)(6). “‘Yard’ means an open space on a lot which is 3 unobstructed from the ground upward except as otherwise provided in this title.” 4 CBMC 17.04.570. “‘Ocean yard’ means a yard measured horizontally at right 5 angles from the most easterly of [the] Oregon Coordinate Line or the western 6 property line, to the nearest point of a building. An ocean yard may be a front 7 yard, a rear yard or a side yard.” CBMC 17.04.578. “For the purpose of 8 determining the oceanfront setback line, the term ‘building’ refers to the 9 residential or commercial structures on a lot. The term ‘building’ does not include 10 accessory structures.” CBMC 17.42.050(A)(6)(b). 11
The only “structures” that are permitted in the ocean yard are fences, decks, 12 or beach access stairs. CBMC 17.42.060(A)(9); CBMC 17.90.070(E).8 With 13

The city reasoned that the proposed dwelling complies 12 with the oceanfront setback, but that the raised elements on the west side of the 13 proposed parking area and vehicular access will result in development that is 14 prohibited in the ocean yard and in the OM overlay. C. Ocean Yard Restrictions 16
With respect to 17.42.050(A)(6), 17.42.060(A)(9), 17.54.030, and 17 17.90.070(E), the city reasoned that the raised elements are “structures” that 18 violate the ocean yard restrictions both on the property and within the Nenana 19 Avenue right-of-way. Record 7. Petitioners argue that city erred in concluding 20 that the raised elements are not permitted in the OM overlay because, according 21 to petitioners, the raised elements are not prohibited “structures” and are, instead, 22 Page 21
retaining walls that are excluded from the definition of “structure” in CBMC 1 17.04.540. Petitioners also argue that the Nenana Avenue right-of-way is not 2 subject to ocean yard restrictions, and so the city may not base its denial on 3 petitioners’ request for approval to develop raised vehicular access in the right-4 of-way. Finally, petitioners argue that, even if the city’s interpretation does not 5 misconstrue the applicable law, and the city’s findings are supported by 6 substantial evidence, the CBMC 17.04.540 definition of the term “structure” is 7 not clear and objective and, thus, may not be applied to deny the application. 8
1. Right-of-way is not subject to “ocean yard” restrictions. 9
It is undisputed that the portion of the Nenana Avenue right-of-way at issue 10 is located within the OM overlay zone. The city council reasoned that the 11 requirements of CBMC 17.42.050, including the oceanfront setback, apply to “all 12 areas contained in the OM [overlay] zone,” and the Nenana Avenue right-of-way 13 is within the OM overlay zone. Record 7. The city council reasoned that their 14 interpretation of CBMC 17.42.050(A)(6) is supported by the language in CBMC 15 17.42.030, which refers to uses and activities permitted “[f]or lots or right-of-16 way” in the OM overlay. 17
We agree with petitioners that the city’s conclusion that city rights-of-way 18 are subject to “ocean yard” restrictions depends on an interpretation of the city’s 19 code that it inconsistent with the code text. The oceanfront setback applies to “all 20 lots abutting the oceanshore,” and is determined by “the location of buildings on 21 lots abutting the oceanshore in the vicinity of the proposed building site.” CBMC 22 Page 22
17.42.050(A)(6)(a) (emphases added). “For the purpose of determining the 1 oceanfront setback line, the term “‘building’ refers to the residential or 2 commercial structures on a lot.” CBMC 17.42.050(A)(6)(b) (emphasis added). 3 The “ocean yard” is defined by reference “to the nearest part of a building.” 4 CBMC 17.04.578. Because the “ocean yard” regulations apply to lots and limit 5 development in the ocean yard, which is defined by buildings “on a lot,” the city’s 6 interpretation that rights-of-way are subject to the ocean yard restrictions is 7 inconsistent with the code’s express language. Accordingly, the city erred in 8 denying petitioners’ application based on the application of the ocean yard 9 restrictions to petitioners’ proposed development in the Nenana Avenue right-of-10 way. 11
2. The term “structure” is impermissibly unclear. 12
A portion of the raised element on the west side of the parking area is 13 within petitioners’ lot, and west, and within the oceanfront setback. The city 14 found that the raised element is a “structure” that is not allowed in the ocean yard. 15 Petitioners argued to the city council that the portion of the raised element in 16 petitioners’ lot is a “retaining wall” that is not a “structure” that is prohibited in 17 the ocean yard. The city rejected that argument and reasoned that only fences, 18 decks, and beach access stairs are allowed within the oceanfront setback under 19 CBMC 17.42.060(A)(9). The city council interpreted “that provision to prohibit 20 all other non-identified structures within the oceanfront setback.” Record 7. 21 Quoting the CBMC 17.04.540 definition of “structure,” the city determined that 22 Page 23
the raised elements are “‘man-made assemblage[s] of materials extending above 1 the surface of the ground,’ both on the lot as well as within the Nenana right-of-2 way.” Record 7 (brackets in original). The city found that the raised element on 3 petitioners’ property “is at least 2 ½ feet above the finished grade, and over four 4 feet above the existing grade of the property.” Id. The city noted that the CBMC 5 does not prescribe the starting point for measuring the height of a retaining wall 6 for purposes of determining whether the retaining wall is a “structure.” The city 7 interpreted the four-foot standard to be measured using the same starting point as 8 “building height” is measured in CBMC 17.04.090, which is “the vertical 9 distance measured from the average elevation of existing grade to the highest 10 point of the [structure].” Record 8.
